content.thinking:
I'm sketching the overall proportions for the scene: a red panda standing on a stone, figuring out realistic sizes for the stone and panda's body so the whole model totals roughly half a meter tall, with everything built facing forward from a ground-level base.

Starting the rig with a hips root joint, then a spine chain running up to chest, neck, and head, plus a separate tail chain, with legs attached via limb joints. For the stone I'm planning to build it from a scaled icosahedron with flat shading rather than a precise lathed shape, positioning it so its base sits right at floor level and its top surface lines up with where the panda's feet will land, then placing the hips and shoulder joints to set up the torso length before working out leg proportions.

For the legs, I'm sketching joint placement and segment lengths given the panda's stocky, short-legged build -- figuring out shoulder and hip joint positions, foot targets, and limb chain lengths so the vertical reach and bend directions work out correctly for both front legs (elbow bending backward) and hind legs (knee forward, hock backward), checking that the summed segment lengths comfortably cover the needed vertical distance.

Now I'm planning the body as a spine chain built from catmull-rom points running from hips through the back to the chest, with a separate neck chain continuing up to the head, giving the head a slight upward tilt for a neutral resting pose. I'm deciding to parent the spine chain to the hips root joint and positioning the path's starting point just forward of the hips so the joints line up naturally.

For color, I'm thinking red panda coloring: rusty back with countershading into a darker belly and legs, wrapped in a cel-shaded fur-edge paint for the fuzzy boundary effect.

For the head, I'm placing a broad skull sphere scaled for wide cheeks on the head bone, then painting face details—rust fur, cream cheeks, white muzzle, dark tear marks—using position-based logic relative to the head center in model space.

Now I'm defining approximate coordinates for the eyes, tear marks, cheek patches, brow highlights, and chin shading, wrapping it all in the cel-shaded paint function, then planning small round amber-brown anime-style eyes as decals on the skull.

Now I'm placing the muzzle and nose shapes, then setting up a separate jaw bone joint so the mouth can articulate relative to the head, aiming it forward and down. For the ears, I'm planning large rounded triangles with rust on the outside and cream on the inner face.

Rather than tying paint color to the sign of s directly, I realize I can just check the world-space normal's z component to decide front versus back faces, since that works symmetrically for both ears regardless of s.

Now I'm shaping the ear outline as a rounded triangle with smoothed corners, and planning the paint logic so front faces get a cream rim with a dark triangular patch near the base.

For the back of the ears I'm going with rust fur transitioning to a darker tip, matching the reference's dark-with-white-rim look. I'm sizing ears roughly 0.1 wide and tall relative to the 0.09-wide head, then turning to cheek fur: I want scattered cream tuft cards at the cheeks using a texture filter, plus similar card-based fur treatment for the rust-colored body.

Now scattering fur tufts across the body — pointed leaf-shaped cards tinted by the coat paint color, with cel-shading applied based on hit normals for lit/shadow variation. Same tuft approach applies to the tail. Then I'm planning the tail itself: a long bushy red panda tail with rings, about 0.45m long tapering to 0.06m radius, built as a bone chain off the hips.

I'm shaping the tail curve so it arcs upward and back without dipping into the stone it's near, sizing segment radii to be thicker mid-tail and thinner near the tip, and setting up ring banding — alternating rust and cream bands based on position along the tail, with a dark brown tip.

For the tail cards, since band color can't use the same sweep parameter there, I'll instead compute the closest point along the tail path for color sampling, using cheaper sweep-based coloring on the tube and path-distance coloring only on the cards to avoid performance issues. Then I'm moving on to legs and paws — dark brown limbs with rounded paw pads, small cream claw cones per foot, and anchoring foot placement to the last joint in each leg's bone chain.

Each leg is a swept chain with tapering radii, hind legs a bit thicker than front, plus a rust-colored thigh bulge sphere at the hip to suggest muscle under the fur. I'm placing front legs under the shoulder joints and hind legs under the lower spine joint, mirroring left/right by name and position, and working out joint coordinates for a standing pose with hips, knees, and feet roughly aligned under the body.

I'm checking the stone's ellipsoid surface math to make sure the feet land naturally on top instead of floating or sinking — the simple single-ellipsoid dome gives too low a top near the edges, so I'm blending in a second flatter ellipsoid lump to approximate a flatter plateau and adjusting foot heights to match where paws would actually rest.

Now I'm layering a mossy stone texture: I'm painting the boulder with noise-driven patches so the top surfaces (facing up) get a mottled green moss color while the rest stays mottled gray stone, then wrapping that in cel shading for the stylized look.

I'm scattering small moss tuft cards across upward-facing stone surfaces using a blade-texture SVG, plus adding tiny decorative details — a few mushrooms, a fallen leaf, small pebbles, and a handful of softly glowing pale-green "dendro mote" spheres floating near the stone for that elemental Genshin touch.

Now I'm adding a Genshin-style accessory: a teal cloth collar with gold trim and tassels looping around the panda's neck, a small gold bell hanging off the front, and a thin gold ring around the tail, all built as sweep loops anchored to the neck and tail joints.

I'm also sketching a hanging triangle bandana flap in teal with a gold hem band along its top edge, deciding to skip extra decal patterns to keep things simple, and reminding myself to watch for unused variables before writing the final code. Next I want to add whiskers as thin cream-white sweeps, a few per side coming off the muzzle.

Still writing spike geometry...

For the small facial details I'm skipping teeth and tongue, considering a tiny dark rod for the mouth line, and placing the head joint's forward offset so I can compute a skull center point usable later for painting.

Now I'm reworking the skull proportions—narrowing the head's half-widths so it matches a red panda's actual width relative to the body, scaling the muzzle and nose smaller, and adjusting eye placement angles. I'm also recalculating the spine and leg joint heights so the body sits higher above the ground, giving the short legs enough visible length while keeping proper hind and front leg segment totals.

Now I'm defining the actual spine point coordinates from hips to neck, setting up the neck as a short two-joint chain parented to the last spine joint, and establishing loft width/height values at each spine station to shape the torso. I'm also planning the fur coloring—rust along the back and neck, cream on the chest—using a paint transition along the body.

Writing body coat paint logic...

For the tail I'm planning ringed bands alternating between a deep rust and tan, with a darker tip at the end, all using cel-shaded coloring.

Now I'm shaping the limbs: scaled spheres for the hip and shoulder, mottled dark fur for the legs, and paw spheres with small claw cones at the front.

Naming joint chains next: hind leg spans need four names including hip, knee, hock, and foot, while the front leg's two spans need shoulder and elbow names leading to the paw tip.

I'm assigning chain roles -- "leg" for hind limbs, "arm" for forelimbs -- plus head, jaw, neck, spine, and tail roles for the main skeleton joints. Then I'm placing ear joints at the base of the head using local offset coordinates and extrusion directions, though I'm second-guessing whether my x/y direction vectors are properly orthogonal.

I'm computing a perpendicular x-axis for the ear extrusion by solving the dot product equation against the y-direction vector, verifying with a cross product that it points outward correctly. I'm deciding to skip extra ear rim detailing and tufts, and moving on to placing eye decals with position and size parameters.

Now I'm setting up stone parts with hip bone attachment and flat geometry, then planning moss cards scattered across stone plateaus using a filtered distribution based on surface normal and minimum distance, with a green blade texture for the moss blades. I'm also starting to design a fur tuft texture using a teardrop-shaped path for body card placement.

Writing fur card texture...

I'm figuring out paint colors for different card regions — coat color for body fur and a cream tone for cheek ruffs on the skull — and defining filter logic based on hit position to decide which cards get the cream tint versus the base coat color.

Still working out card placement...

Now I'm planning the tail cards using a Catmull-Rom path and closest-point paint lookup for gradient coloring along the tail, then sanity-checking the total card and triangle counts before moving on to the gold collar.

For the collar, I want to find a plane through a point along the neck chain to cut the neck sweep surface and generate a loop for the collar geometry, choosing a point partway along the neck so the plane only intersects the neck tube and not the body.

Now I'm adding gold trim rings as thin loops near the neck, plus a small gold bell sphere positioned near the collar's midpoint using the neck joint as its bone reference, and sketching a triangular bandana flap extruded from the collar's bottom edge.

Checking the chest front depth against the neck-and-collar geometry, the flap's z-position might slightly embed into the torso loft, but that's acceptable since it'll just float near the surface without a visible gap.

Now I'm designing the flap's gold trim: a chevron-style border using a width function that tapers linearly for y between 0 and -0.02, deciding paint color based on whether a point falls near the triangular edge versus the teal interior.

Beyond that, I'm adding glowing dendro-style motes scattered near the body, a gold ring sweep around the tail, and small mushroom props near the stone's edge, with lathe-built caps colored reddish-orange and spotted with cream dots, mounted on thin cream stems.

For placement, I'm raycasting down onto the stone surface to find valid landing points so mushrooms sit flush with the rock contours, skipping any failed hits. Then I'm defining the stone's material with a noise-based blend between mossy green patches and faceted gray rock tones, using a height and noise function to decide the mix so moss clusters lower and rock dominates higher up.

Now I'm assembling the stone geometry itself—an icosahedron base with scaled lumps and a plateau positioned to support the figure's feet—carefully checking the surface heights at each foot position so paws sink just slightly into the rock before the moss cards cover the seam.

For legs I'm defining bend directions for the limb chains, with front legs bending back at the elbow and hind legs bending through a double joint. Then I'm setting up the jaw joint attached near the head's forward-down position, adding a cream jaw bone, a small dark interior mouth shape, and finally placing the head joint at the end of the neck path.

Now I'm working through the finer facial details: the nose as a small dark glossy bump, cream brow patches, cheek cards, dark ear interiors, and whiskers built as spikes radiating from the muzzle with slightly varying length and angle per row. I'm also adding a thin dark mouth line rod running from the nose down to the chin area, then moving on to start writing the actual code with the necessary imports.

Setting up colors and fur paints for the body...

Settling on a smooth tail radius array for a bushy curl shape with four spans, then starting the actual module setup: importing builder, math, path, IK, paint, and toon/glow kits, and beginning the build function with metadata and the root hips joint for the red panda's spine chain.

Now I'm defining the spine chain with catmull-spline points and four named joints, then branching off a neck chain from the final spine joint. I'm building the body as a lofted mesh following the spine path with varying width/height per station, adding a swept neck tube, and starting to construct the skull geometry.

For the face coloring, I'm writing a paint function that checks distances from the head center along each axis to decide where muzzle/chin cream patches go, where the dark tear-mark stripes run from eyes to mouth, where cheek cream patches sit, and where the brow markings appear, falling back to the rust fur color everywhere else -- ordering the conditions so tear marks get checked before the muzzle cream to avoid overlap conflicts.

Now I'm setting up the eyes with an anime-style iris color and default sizing, placing eye decals on the skull surface mirrored left/right, then building the ear joints as hinges attached to the head with positions offset up and to the side, and extruding the ear shape outward from that base point.

For the ear paint, I'm defining color rules based on surface normal and position: the front-facing side gets cream with a dark inner ring near the base, while the back gets mostly dark brown with a rust patch near the base. The outline for the ear is a small convex polygon roughly a tenth of the head's width, extruded with a slight bevel to give it thickness.

Now I'm moving on to the legs. I'm setting up mottled fur coloring for the limbs, then looping over left and right sides to compute shoulder and hip joint positions relative to the body, building front and hind limb chains with appropriate reach distances and joint counts, and naming each joint (shoulder, elbow, hand) per side.

Then I'm adding paw spheres with dark toe accents, three small claw spikes angled outward from each toe using directional vectors, and separate toe bump spheres for visual detail, positioning everything relative to the hand or foot tip bones before repeating the same paw/toe/claw setup for the hind limbs.

I'm sketching the hind thigh and chest bulge spheres with coat-colored shading tied to their respective joint bones, then moving on to building the body surface scatter and a separate stone surface with moss scattering filtered by normal direction and height, using randomized leaning and texture size for the moss patches.

Now I'm designing the moss tuft texture as an SVG with several overlapping blade shapes in varying green tones, then setting up mushroom placement logic: raycasting down onto the stone surface to find base positions, then building stem rods and lathed caps with spotted coloring, sized to keep each mushroom around 4cm tall with a cream stem and reddish-orange cap.

Writing lathe outline coordinates...

I'm planning the gold trim details across the panda — a teal collar loop with gold accent loops at different points along the neck sweep, a bell hanging from the collar midpoint, and a gold tail ring positioned partway along the tail. I'm also sketching out the mouth geometry using small rods for the nose-to-mouth line and symmetric smile curves, checking type signatures for surface scattering, hit raycasting, and part-to-surface conversions, and confirming paint and chain definitions are ordered correctly before I commit everything to the file.
